title: A perfect storm of turbulent gases
caption: Part of the Omega Nebula, Messier 17, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 17 · constellation Sagittarius · about 5500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: European Space Agency, NASA, and J. Hester (Arizona State University)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Like a raging sea, a bubbly ocean of glowing gas fills this Hubble view of a small region inside Messier 17, also called the Omega or Swan Nebula. The nebula is a hotbed of star formation about 5500 light-years away in Sagittarius, and this patch is roughly 3 light-years across.

The wave-like shapes were sculpted and lit by a flood of ultraviolet light from young, massive stars that sit outside the picture, to the upper left. Their glow reveals the three-dimensional structure of the gas. The radiation is eroding and warming the outer layers of cold hydrogen clouds, and those warmed surfaces glow orange and red here.

Heat and pressure drive some material off those surfaces, forming a veil of even hotter gas, shown in green, which hides structures behind it. The pressure on the crests of the waves may be enough to trigger new stars inside them.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.79 x 1.46 arcminutes) and distance (5500 light years), the frame spans roughly 2.9 × 2.3 light-years. Its light set out about 5,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2. The colours represent different gases: red for sulphur, green for hydrogen and blue for oxygen.
understand.eye: The colours are assigned to individual gases, so they map chemistry rather than the natural hues an eye would see.

alt: Wave-like clouds of glowing gas in orange, red and green, resembling a stormy sea.
